labs.title: Lab 1 — Joiner-Mover-Leaver & Access Governance
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.6 Implement and maintain identity and access management (provisioning/deprovisioning, RBAC, ABAC, least privilege).
  • 5.1 Security governance (separation of duties, policies, procedures).
  • 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity (privilege creep, orphaned accounts).

What this lab simulates

An HR feed drives the identity lifecycle:

  • Joiner – a new identity is created and birthright access is provisioned from its role (RBAC).
  • Mover – a role/department change. Correct behaviour: revoke the old role's permissions. Leaving them in place causes privilege creep.
  • Leaver – the account is disabled, every entitlement is revoked and a deprovisioning ticket is generated (with an SLA).

Every access decision passes two gates:

1. RBAC – does any of the user's roles grant the permission? 2. ABAC – do the *attributes* (employment status, clearance vs. data classification, department, time of day) allow it?

Finally a Separation of Duties scan flags users who hold two permissions that should never be combined (e.g. po:create + po:approve).

Run it

python main.py lab 1

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.6 (IAM: provisioning, RBAC/ABAC, least privilege) and 5.1 (separation of duties).
concepts: RBAC grants permissions through job roles; ABAC adds context (clearance, department, time, status).
Least privilege: a Mover must LOSE the old role's rights, not just gain the new ones.
Separation of Duties prevents one person completing a sensitive transaction end-to-end.
Leaver processing: disable first, then revoke, then reclaim assets; keep the account for legal hold.
failure_modes: Privilege creep: movers keep old roles; 'temporary' grants never expire.
Orphaned accounts: HR never tells IT, so ex-employees keep VPN/SSO access.
Terminations for cause handled at normal SLA — the user has hours to exfiltrate data.
SoD conflicts invisible because nobody reviews the COMBINED permission set.
ai_governance: An AI provisioning agent should only act on events from the authoritative HR source.
Require human approval for any grant that would create an SoD conflict.
Agents must never be able to grant roles to themselves or their own service account.
Log every agent-initiated change with the triggering HR event ID for audit traceability.
exam_tips: 'Users accumulate permissions over time' => privilege creep => fix with access reviews/recertification.
'Same employee creates and approves payments' => separation of duties.
'Access based on attributes like location or time' => ABAC.
Mandatory vacation and job rotation are detective controls that also expose SoD fraud.

labs.title: Lab 2 — Zero Trust Access Evaluator (PE / PA / PEP)
labs.objectives: SY0-701 1.2 Zero Trust control & data planes · 4.6 Conditional access
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 1.2 Zero Trust: Control Plane (adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, policy-driven access control, Policy Engine, Policy Administrator) and Data Plane (implicit trust zones, subject/system, Policy Enforcement Point).
  • 4.6 Context-aware / conditional access, MFA.

Architecture (NIST SP 800-207)

:

Subject ──request──▶ PEP ──▶ Policy Engine (PE)  ─ decides (trust algorithm)
                      ▲          │
                      │          ▼
                      └──── Policy Administrator (PA) ─ issues/revokes tokens
(data plane)              (control plane)
  • PE scores every request using context: identity risk, MFA, device posture, IP reputation, geo, time of day, resource sensitivity.
  • PA turns the PE verdict into an action: mint a short-lived, scoped, HMAC-signed token, require step-up MFA, or deny. It can also revoke.
  • PEP sits in front of the resource and enforces: no valid token, no data. It checks signature, expiry, scope and revocation on *every* request — "never trust, always verify".

Run it

python main.py lab 2

insight.objective: SY0-701 1.2 Zero Trust (control plane vs data plane) and 4.6 conditional access.
concepts: Control plane = Policy Engine (decides) + Policy Administrator (issues/revokes). Data plane = PEP + resources.
Adaptive identity: the same user gets ALLOW, STEP_UP or DENY depending on real-time context.
Threat scope reduction: tokens are short-lived and scoped to ONE resource + action.
Never trust, always verify: the PEP re-validates on every request, even inside the network.
failure_modes: Treating 'on the VPN' or 'inside the LAN' as trusted (implicit trust zone).
Long-lived or broadly-scoped tokens enable replay and lateral movement.
MFA push approval alone treated as proof — MFA fatigue attacks bypass it.
No revocation path: compromised sessions stay valid until expiry.
ai_governance: Treat every AI agent as a non-human SUBJECT with its own identity, entitlements and device/workload posture.
Agents should receive short-lived, narrowly-scoped tokens per task — never standing credentials.
The PE should weigh agent-specific risk signals (anomalous call volume, new tool usage).
The PA must be able to revoke an agent's tokens instantly (kill switch).
exam_tips: 'Component that makes the access decision' => Policy Engine. 'Component that enforces it' => PEP.
'Establishes and terminates the session / issues tokens' => Policy Administrator.
Zero Trust replaces perimeter trust with continuous, per-request verification.
Microsegmentation and implicit trust zones are data-plane concepts.

labs.title: Lab 3 — Log Forensic Inspector & Hash Verifier
labs.objectives: SY0-701 4.9 Investigation data sources · 2.4 Indicators · 1.4 Hashing
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.9 Use data sources to support an investigation (firewall, OS/Windows event, application, endpoint logs; SIEM; metadata).
  • 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity (brute force, impossible travel, account lockout, blocked content, out-of-cycle logging, missing logs).
  • 1.4 Hashing & salting for integrity.
  • 4.8 Incident response — chain of custody / evidence integrity.

Pipeline

1. Parse heterogeneous raw lines (firewall, Windows Event, web, EDR) into one normalised schema (what a SIEM's parser/normaliser does). 2. Enrich with offline GeoIP so location-based rules work. 3. Detect with correlation rules: brute force (Event ID 4625 bursts), password spray, success-after-failure, impossible travel, port scans, threat-intel matches (IP / user agent / hash), SQL injection, audit-log clearing (Event ID 1102). 4. Extract IOCs (IPs, hashes, user agents, domains) by regex. 5. Verify integrity of the log set using a salted SHA-256 hash chain and an HMAC-signed manifest — detects edited, deleted or injected lines.

Run it

python main.py lab 3
python main.py lab 3 --file my_logs.json

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.9 (investigation data sources), 2.4 (indicators of malicious activity), 1.4 (hashing).
concepts: Event ID 4625 = failed logon, 4624 = success, 4672 = special privileges, 1102 = Security log cleared.
Correlation turns weak signals into strong ones: 4625 burst + 4624 from the same IP = compromise.
Impossible travel compares geo distance / time between logons for one identity.
A salted hash chain makes logs tamper-EVIDENT; an HMAC proves who sealed the manifest.
failure_modes: Reviewing each log source in isolation, so the cross-source story is missed.
Alerting on 4625 per user only — password spray (one IP, many users) slips under lockout thresholds.
Collecting evidence without hashing it, breaking chain of custody in court.
Not alerting on Event 1102 or on hosts that suddenly stop logging.
ai_governance: An AI SOC agent may triage and enrich, but must cite the exact log lines (evidence) behind every claim.
Agents must have READ-ONLY access to logs — never delete, rotate or modify audit data.
Verify integrity before an agent analyses logs; poisoned logs = poisoned conclusions.
Containment actions (blocking an IP, disabling an account) should require human approval on high-impact assets.
exam_tips: 'Many failed logins for many accounts from one source' => password spraying.
'User logged in from two countries 30 minutes apart' => impossible travel.
'Prove evidence was not altered' => hashing / chain of custody.
Missing or out-of-cycle logs are themselves an indicator of compromise.

labs.title: Lab 4 — Change Control & Impact Analyzer (CAB)
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 1.3 Change management: approval process, ownership, stakeholders, impact analysis, test results, backout plan, maintenance window, SOPs; technical implications (allow/deny lists, restricted activities, downtime, service/application restarts, legacy applications, dependencies); documentation & version control.
  • 5.1 Governance — separation of duties in approvals.

What this lab does

Each Request for Change (RFC) is reviewed the way a Change Advisory Board would:

1. Schedule — inside an approved maintenance window? on a blackout date? 2. Approvals — CAB quorum met? did the requester approve their own change? 3. Testing — was it validated in staging? 4. Impact analysis — blast radius through the dependency graph, legacy systems broken by disabled protocols, services cut off by deny-list rules, restarts causing downtime. 5. Backout validation — every reversible step has an undo; irreversible steps have a backup first and a fail-forward plan; the plan fits the window. 6. Execution rehearsal — the change is *executed* against a simulated environment, failed on purpose, and the backout is run to prove the system returns to its original state.

Run it

python main.py lab 4
python main.py lab 4 --file my_rfcs.json

insight.objective: SY0-701 1.3 Change management processes and their technical implications.
concepts: Change process: request → impact analysis → test → CAB approval → schedule in window → implement → verify → document.
Impact analysis must follow the DEPENDENCY graph — the patched box is rarely the one that breaks.
Backout (rollback) restores the prior state; fail-forward fixes forward when rollback is impossible.
Allow/deny-list changes, service restarts and legacy applications are the classic technical implications.
failure_modes: Hardening a protocol (e.g. disabling TLS 1.0) that an undocumented legacy app still needs.
A backout plan that exists on paper but was never rehearsed — it fails at 3 a.m.
Requester approves their own change, or 'everyone' approves without owner sign-off.
Change + rollback takes longer than the maintenance window → uncoordinated downtime.
ai_governance: An AI patching agent must submit RFCs and wait for CAB approval — it must not self-approve.
Require the agent to output an impact analysis and a machine-executable backout plan with every RFC.
Agents may only execute inside an approved window and must auto-trigger backout on failed health checks.
Irreversible actions (schema migrations, data purges, firmware) always need a human at the keyboard.
exam_tips: 'Plan to restore the system if the change fails' => backout plan.
'Who approves changes' => Change Advisory Board (CAB); emergency changes go through an ECAB.
'Scheduled time to make changes with minimal business impact' => maintenance window.
Legacy applications and dependencies are listed explicitly as technical implications in 1.3.

labs.title: Lab 5 — AI Agent Supervisor & Guardrail Governor
labs.objectives: SY0-701 4.7 Automation guardrails · 4.6 Non-human PAM · 5.1 Human-in-the-loop
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives (applied to autonomous agents)

  • 4.7 Automation & orchestration — guardrails, ticketing, escalation, "single point of failure", complexity and technical-debt risks.
  • 4.6 Least privilege and privileged access management for NON-HUMAN identities.
  • 1.3 Change management — automated changes still require approval.
  • 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity — runaway or hijacked automation.
  • 5.1 Governance — human-in-the-loop, accountability, audit.

The model

AI agents never touch production directly. Each proposed action is sent to the Governor (a policy decision point for automation) which returns:

  • ALLOW – inside every boundary; executes automatically.
  • REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL – plausible but high-impact/uncertain; queued for HITL.
  • BLOCK – violates a hard boundary; never executes.

Checks performed (in order)

1. Agent identity & quarantine status (kill switch) 2. Least privilege — is this action type in the agent's allow-list? 3. Hallucination detection — non-existent assets, patches, or CAB tickets 4. Hard security boundaries — immutable firewall rule 0, protected controls (MFA/EDR/audit logging), audit-log tampering, self-privilege escalation, admin grants without an approved CAB ticket 5. Dangerous command patterns (curl | sh, rm -rf / ...) 6. Prompt-injection indicators in the agent's own justification 7. Rate limiting (runaway agent) 8. Confidence threshold & critical-asset escalation → human-in-the-loop

Every decision is written to a hash-chained ledger so the audit trail of what the automation tried to do is itself tamper-evident.

Run it

python main.py lab 5
python main.py lab 5 --file my_agent_actions.json

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.7 (automation & orchestration guardrails) + 4.6 PAM for non-human identities + 5.1 oversight.
concepts: Every agent is a non-human identity with its own least-privilege allow-list — never a shared admin account.
Three-tier verdicts: ALLOW (in policy), REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL (uncertain/high impact), BLOCK (hard boundary).
Hard boundaries are non-overridable: even a human can't approve disabling MFA through the agent pipeline.
A kill switch (quarantine) stops runaway or hijacked automation after repeated violations.
failure_modes: Giving the agent a domain-admin service account 'so it can do its job' (no blast-radius limit).
Trusting the agent's own references: it can invent ticket numbers, patch IDs and hostnames.
Indirect prompt injection — data the agent reads (tickets, emails, logs) tells it to break policy.
No rate limit: a looping agent restarts production 400 times before anyone notices.
ai_governance: Validate every agent claim against an authoritative source (CMDB, patch catalog, ticketing system).
Route privileged or irreversible actions through the same CAB/approval workflow as humans.
Keep a tamper-evident ledger of every proposed AND executed action for accountability.
Separate duties: the agent that proposes a change must not be the identity that approves it.
exam_tips: Automation benefits: enforcing baselines, standard configurations, scaling securely, reaction time.
Automation risks listed in 4.7: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt, ongoing supportability.
'Guard rails' in 4.7 = automated limits that keep scripts/agents inside safe boundaries.
Human-in-the-loop is the governance answer whenever impact is high and confidence is low.

labs.title: Lab 6 — Risk Management Calculator & BIA
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 5.2 Risk management: identification, assessment (qualitative/quantitative), SLE, ALE, ARO, exposure factor, risk register, risk owner, risk appetite/tolerance, risk thresholds, strategies (transfer, accept, exemption/exception, avoid, mitigate), business impact analysis (RTO, RPO, MTTR, MTBF).

Formulas

SLE = AV × EF            (single loss expectancy)
ALE = SLE × ARO          (annualized loss expectancy)
Control value = ALE_before − ALE_after − annual control cost
Availability  = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)

Treatment logic

1. ALE within risk appetite → ACCEPT (document it; the risk owner signs). 2. Otherwise compute the net annual benefit of every option:

  • MITIGATE = ALE − ALE_after_control − control cost
  • TRANSFER = ALE × insurance coverage − premium
  • AVOID = ALE − cost of stopping the activity (only if the activity is optional)

3. Choose the option with the best positive benefit. If none is positive, the risk stays above appetite and needs a formal EXCEPTION signed by leadership.

Run it

python main.py lab 6

insight.objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative analysis, strategies, BIA).
concepts: SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE reduction > its annual cost.
Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity), accept, or exception/exemption.
RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how long you can be down (drives restore design).
MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
failure_modes: Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security theatre).
Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead of transferring them.
Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours, discovered only after an outage.
Risks accepted informally with no owner, no expiry date and no register entry.
ai_governance: An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a named human risk OWNER must accept.
Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can be audited and challenged.
AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure, prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a compromise. Price that in.
exam_tips: Expect arithmetic: AV $100k, EF 25%, ARO 2 → SLE $25k, ALE $50k.
'Purchasing cyber insurance' = transfer. 'Discontinuing the service' = avoid.
'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to restore' = RTO.
Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance = acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.

labs.title: Lab 7 — Incident Response Runner & Chain of Custody
labs.objectives: SY0-701 4.8 Incident response & digital forensics · 4.9 Data sources
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.8 Incident response: process (preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned), training, testing (tabletop, simulation), root cause analysis, threat hunting, digital forensics (legal hold, chain of custody, acquisition, reporting, preservation, e-discovery).
  • 4.9 Data sources supporting an investigation.

What this lab does

You give it a *playbook*: an ordered list of response actions picked from a catalog. The grader then checks it:

  • Lifecycle order — containment before eradication, eradication before recovery, lessons learned at the end, no containment after recovery.
  • Order of volatility (RFC 3227) — collect CPU/RAM/network state before disk, and disk before remote logs and archives.
  • Evidence destruction — powering off or reimaging before acquisition destroys evidence permanently.
  • Prerequisites — e.g. no reimage without a disk image and a legal hold.
  • Chain of custody — every evidence item is hashed at acquisition and logged to a tamper-evident custody ledger.

The sample compares a rookie response with an expert one.

Run it

python main.py lab 7
python main.py lab 7 --file my_incident.json   # grade your own playbook

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.8 Incident response process & digital forensics.
concepts: Lifecycle: preparation → detection → analysis → containment → eradication → recovery → lessons learned.
Order of volatility (RFC 3227): registers/cache → RAM & network state → swap/temp → disk → remote logs → archives.
Chain of custody: who collected what, when, with which hash, and every hand-off since. One gap and the evidence can be thrown out.
A legal hold freezes deletion of relevant data the moment litigation is reasonably anticipated.
failure_modes: Pulling the plug 'to stop the malware': RAM-resident malware and network state are gone forever.
Reimaging before imaging the disk: no root cause analysis, no evidence for law enforcement or insurers.
Restoring service before eradication: re-infection from the persistence you never found.
Skipping lessons learned, so the playbook never improves.
ai_governance: AI responders should follow the SAME lifecycle; enforce phase gates (no eradication until containment is confirmed).
Agents may collect evidence but must hash it at acquisition and write to an append-only custody ledger.
Destructive actions (power off, reimage, delete) need human sign-off and must check that evidence was acquired first.
Log every agent action into the incident timeline; the agent's own actions are evidence too.
exam_tips: 'What should be collected first?' → the most volatile source available (usually RAM).
'Stop the spread' = containment; 'remove the malware' = eradication; 'return to normal' = recovery.
'Documents everyone who handled the evidence' = chain of custody.
Tabletop exercise = discussion-based; simulation = hands-on practice of the plan.

labs.title: Lab 8 — End-to-End SOC Pipeline (Detect → Agent → Governor → CAB / IAM / IR)
labs.objectives: SY0-701 4.7 SOAR · 4.8 IR · 1.3 Emergency change · 4.6 IAM · 1.2 Zero Trust
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.7 Automation & orchestration (SOAR): playbooks, guardrails, escalation.
  • 4.8 Incident response · 4.9 Investigation data sources
  • 1.3 Change management for emergency changes · 4.6 IAM · 1.2 Zero Trust

The architecture this whole engine builds toward

:

Lab 3 Detect ──▶ AI SOC agent proposes ──▶ Lab 5 Governor ──▶ human (HITL)
                                               │
                 ┌─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
                 ▼                             ▼                          ▼
      disable_account                     block_ip                   isolate_host
  Lab 1 IGA suspend + Lab 2         Lab 4 emergency RFC → CAB     Lab 7 IR case: capture
  PA revokes every session          review + rehearsed backout    volatile evidence FIRST

The "AI agent" here is a deterministic stand-in that maps findings to proposed actions, including one overreach that the Governor must stop. Replace soc_agent_propose with a real model and every guardrail still applies.

Run it

python main.py lab 8

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.7 Automation & orchestration (SOAR) tying together 1.2, 1.3, 4.6, 4.8 and 4.9.
concepts: Detection, decision and execution are separate trust boundaries; no single component (or agent) owns all three.
Every automated action is routed to the control that owns it: IAM for accounts, CAB for network changes, IR for hosts.
Emergency changes still get an RFC, ECAB approval, a rehearsed backout and a post-implementation review.
Human-in-the-loop on user-impacting actions turns false positives into rule-tuning instead of outages.
failure_modes: A SOAR playbook that disables accounts automatically locks out the CEO on a false positive.
Automation that blocks IPs directly on the firewall, bypassing change control: no backout, no record.
Isolating or wiping a host before capturing memory destroys the evidence that explains the breach.
An over-privileged agent 'containing' an incident by changing the default firewall rule.
ai_governance: Give the SOC agent a narrow allow-list and let it PROPOSE; the Governor and humans DISPOSE.
Make every downstream system (IAM, CAB, IR) enforce its own rules even for approved agent actions: defense in depth.
Feed human rejections back as tuning data, e.g. the travel-VPN egress that triggered impossible travel.
Measure the agent: precision of its proposals, how often humans overturn it, and blocked attempts.
exam_tips: SOAR = Security Orchestration, Automation and Response: playbooks that act on SIEM alerts.
Benefits in 4.7: efficiency, enforcing baselines, reaction time, workforce multiplier.
Considerations in 4.7: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt, ongoing supportability.
Containment choices (isolate, segment, disable) must balance evidence preservation against spread.

labs.title: Lab 9 — Vulnerability Triage & Remediation
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.3 Vulnerability management: identification (scans, threat feeds), analysis (confirmation, prioritisation, CVSS, CVE, classification, exposure factor, environmental variables, industry/organisational impact, risk tolerance), response & remediation (patching, insurance, segmentation, compensating controls, exceptions/exemptions), validation (rescanning, audit, verification), reporting.
  • 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities (injection, buffer overflow, race condition, malicious update, end-of-life, misconfiguration, cryptographic, zero-day…).

Prioritisation model

score = CVSS base × criticality multiplier (CMDB tier 1–5)
                  × KEV multiplier (known exploited in the wild)
                  × exposure multiplier (internet / privileged / internal)

P1 ≥ 12 · P2 ≥ 8 · P3 ≥ 4 · otherwise P4    → SLA 7 / 30 / 90 / 180 days
KEV findings never get more than 14 days (CISA BOD 22-01 style).

Deny by default: an asset that is NOT in the CMDB is scored as worst case (criticality 5, internet-facing) until someone registers and owns it.

Exceptions are accepted only if ALL hold: authorised approver, not expired, duration ≤ 180 days, recognised compensating controls, and the residual score after those controls is ≤ 8 (P3 or lower).

Run it

python main.py lab 9

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.3 Vulnerability management (analysis, prioritisation, remediation, validation) and 2.3 vulnerability types.
concepts: CVSS is a severity score, not a risk score. Risk adds asset criticality, exposure and active exploitation (KEV).
Remediation options: patch, segment/isolate, compensating controls, insurance, or a time-boxed exception.
Validation closes the loop: rescan, audit or verify. A ticket marked 'done' is not proof.
Assets missing from the inventory are the most dangerous: nobody patches what nobody owns.
failure_modes: Sorting by CVSS alone, so a 9.8 on a lab box outranks a KEV 7.5 on an internet-facing gateway.
Exceptions with no expiry, approved by whoever asked, renewed forever.
Waiting for a patch on a zero-day instead of applying compensating controls today.
Closing findings without rescanning: the patch failed silently.
ai_governance: An AI triage agent may score and rank findings, but exceptions need an authorised human risk owner.
Agents must take criticality and exposure from the CMDB, never infer or invent them; unknown assets mean worst case.
Auto-patching agents go through change control (Lab 4) and must trigger a validation rescan afterwards.
Log the agent's scoring inputs so a human can reproduce any priority it assigns.
exam_tips: CVSS bands: 9.0–10 Critical, 7.0–8.9 High, 4.0–6.9 Medium, 0.1–3.9 Low.
'Cannot patch, so add a control that reduces the risk' = compensating control.
'Formally accept a vulnerability for a defined time' = exception/exemption.
TOC/TOU = race condition; malicious update = supply chain; no vendor fix yet = zero-day.

labs.title: Lab 10 — Email Security Analyzer (SPF / DKIM / DMARC / phishing)
labs.objectives: SY0-701 4.5 Email security · 2.2 Message-based threat vectors
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.5 Email security: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, gateway, secure/MIME.
  • 2.2 Threat vectors & attack surfaces: message-based (email), phishing, business email compromise, impersonation, brand impersonation, typosquatting, file-based (malicious attachments).

What the analyzer does

1. Parses raw RFC 5322 messages with the standard library email package. 2. Re-computes authentication itself against an offline DNS table:

  • SPF: connecting IP (from our own MX's Received header) vs the envelope domain's v=spf1 record (ip4:, include:, -all/~all).
  • DKIM: recomputes the body hash (simple canonicalisation, SHA-256) and compares it with bh=; checks the selector key is published. (Signature RSA maths is out of scope; body integrity + key presence is modelled.)
  • DMARC: passes if SPF *or* DKIM passes and is aligned with the From domain (relaxed: same organisational domain), then applies p=. A sender-supplied Authentication-Results header is never trusted; if it claims "pass" where we computed "fail", that itself is an indicator.

3. Scores indicators: lookalike/brand domains, display-name impersonation of executives or brands, Reply-To mismatch, urgency/credential/payment keywords, risky links (IP literal, shortener, punycode, anchor/href mismatch, suspicious TLD), dangerous or double-extension attachments. 4. Verdict, deny by default: REJECT / QUARANTINE / DELIVER_WITH_BANNER / DELIVER, plus an attack category.

Run it

python main.py lab 10

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.5 Email security (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, gateways) and 2.2 message-based threat vectors.
concepts: SPF authorises sending IPs for the ENVELOPE domain; DKIM signs the message for the d= domain.
DMARC ties them to the visible From: SPF or DKIM must pass AND align with the From domain; p= says what to do on failure.
Authentication proves where mail came from, not that it is safe: a lookalike domain can pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
Content signals (impersonation, urgency, mismatched links, double extensions) catch what authentication cannot.
failure_modes: Publishing DMARC p=none forever: you can see the spoofing but never block it.
Trusting an Authentication-Results header added by an untrusted hop.
Allowing external mail whose display name matches the CEO, with no 'external sender' banner.
Blocking .exe but not .pdf.exe, .iso, .lnk or macro-enabled documents.
ai_governance: An AI mail-triage agent may quarantine and add banners; releasing quarantined mail or allow-listing senders needs a human.
Mail content is untrusted input: an email that tells the agent to 'mark this sender safe' is prompt injection.
Agents must base verdicts on recomputed SPF/DKIM/DMARC, never on headers the sender controls.
Log every agent verdict with its indicators so false positives can be tuned, as in the Lab 8 feedback loop.
exam_tips: SPF = which servers may send · DKIM = digital signature on the message · DMARC = policy + alignment + reporting.
BEC/impersonation: 'CEO' from a free-mail address asking for a wire transfer or changed bank details.
Typosquatting / brand impersonation: micros0ft-support.com, paypa1.com.
Secure email gateways enforce these checks at the perimeter; S/MIME provides end-to-end signing/encryption.

labs.title: Lab 11 — Firewall Rule & Network Segmentation Auditor
labs.objectives: SY0-701 3.2 Secure infrastructure (zones, screened subnet) · 4.5 Firewall rules & ACLs
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 3.2 Secure enterprise infrastructure: security zones, attack surface, device placement (DMZ/screened subnet), firewalls, ACLs, fail-closed.
  • 4.5 Modify enterprise capabilities: firewall rules, access lists, ports/protocols, screened subnets, implicit deny.

How rules are modelled

A rule {id, action, src, dst, proto, ports, log, comment} matches a set of traffic. src/dst are a zone name, a CIDR or any; zones (and their CIDRs) come from the ruleset. Because each rule is a *set*, the auditor can prove relationships between rules:

  • SHADOWED: an earlier rule with the OPPOSITE action fully covers this one, so it can never take effect (e.g. a deny after a broader allow).
  • REDUNDANT: an earlier rule with the SAME action fully covers it.
  • ANY_ANY: allow any source → any destination on any port.
  • ANY_SERVICE: allow on every port (not least privilege).
  • SEGMENTATION_VIOLATION: allowed zone-to-zone flow not in the policy (e.g. internet → internal, guest → internal).
  • INSECURE_PROTOCOL: cleartext protocols anywhere; remote-admin ports from untrusted zones.
  • OVERLY_BROAD: huge CIDR (e.g. /8) spanning several zones.
  • MISSING_DEFAULT_DENY: no explicit, logged deny any any at the end.
  • NO_LOGGING / UNDOCUMENTED: deny without logging; rule without a comment.

Score = 100 − Σ penalties, then grade A–F, with a fix for every finding.

Run it

python main.py lab 11

insight.objective: SY0-701 3.2 secure infrastructure (zones, screened subnets) and 4.5 firewall rules / ACLs.
concepts: Rules are evaluated top-down, first match wins, so ORDER is part of the security policy.
Implicit deny: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked. Make it explicit and logged.
Screened subnet (DMZ): internet → DMZ on published ports only; DMZ → internal only to specific back-end services.
Least privilege for networks: specific source, destination, protocol and port, never 'any' for convenience.
failure_modes: A 'temporary' any/any rule added during troubleshooting and never removed.
A new deny rule appended to the bottom, below an allow that already matches the traffic (shadowed).
RDP or SMB opened to the internet 'for a vendor'.
Rule sets nobody can explain because rules carry no owner, ticket or comment.
ai_governance: An AI firewall agent should submit proposed rules to this audit + change control (Lab 4) before deployment.
Block agents from creating any/any or segmentation-violating rules (Lab 5 OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_RULE).
Agents must never edit the default-deny or other immutable rules (Lab 5 rule 0).
Require every agent-created rule to carry a ticket reference and an expiry for temporary access.
exam_tips: 'Rule never matches because an earlier rule catches the traffic' = shadowed rule.
'Last rule of an ACL that blocks everything else' = implicit deny.
Screened subnet = DMZ; place public-facing servers there, not on the internal network.
Fail-closed (secure) vs fail-open (available): know which a firewall/IPS should use for the scenario.

labs.title: Lab 12 — Secure Baseline & Hardening Checker
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.1 Apply common security techniques to computing resources: secure baselines (establish, deploy, maintain), hardening targets (servers, workstations, network devices…), password policy, removal of unnecessary services/software, logging/auditing, host firewall, EDR, patching, configuration enforcement.

What it does

Each host profile (windows_server, linux_server) has a CIS-style baseline in config/default_policies.json → hardening_baselines. A check is {setting, op, value} with ops eq, ge, le, between, includes (list must contain all values) and excludes (list must contain none of them).

For every host the checker reports:

  • PASS / FAIL / MISSING / EXCEPTION per check. MISSING means the setting wasn't reported and counts as a failure (deny by default). EXCEPTION is a documented, ticketed, unexpired deviation.
  • Weighted compliance % (high 10, medium 5, low 2). A host is COMPLIANT only if it scores ≥ 90% AND has no failed high-severity checks.
  • Drift against the previous approved scan: REGRESSED (pass → fail) and REMEDIATED (fail → pass).
  • Remediation steps taken from the baseline.

Run it

python main.py lab 12

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain; hardening targets and techniques.
concepts: A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration; deploy it with GPO/MDM/config management, then measure drift.
Hardening = reduce attack surface: remove unneeded services, enforce password/lockout policy, enable host firewall, EDR and auditing.
Unknown is non-compliant: a setting the scanner can't read is treated as failed until proven otherwise.
Exceptions are documented, ticketed, compensated and time-boxed, never silent.
failure_modes: Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration drift goes unnoticed.
Someone re-enables Print Spooler on a domain controller 'to print one report' (PrintNightmare).
Turning off the host firewall or EDR to troubleshoot and never turning it back on.
Baselines kept in a PDF instead of enforced as code.
ai_governance: A remediation agent may apply baseline settings, but only via change control with rollback (Lab 4).
Agents must never weaken a baseline (disable firewall/EDR/auditing); that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
Drift alerts are a great agent job: detect, explain, open a ticket, attach the remediation step.
Approving a deviation (exception) stays a human decision with an expiry date.
exam_tips: 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic hardening.
Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline; detect with periodic scans.
Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control) both appear in 4.1.

labs.title: Lab 13 — Threat Actor & Attack Vector Classifier
labs.objectives: SY0-701 2.1 Threat actors & motivations · 2.2 Threat vectors · 2.5 Mitigations
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 2.1 Threat actors (nation-state, unskilled attacker, hacktivist, insider threat, organized crime, shadow IT), their attributes (internal/external, resources/funding, sophistication) and motivations (data exfiltration, espionage, service disruption, blackmail, financial gain, philosophical/ political beliefs, ethical, revenge, disruption/chaos, war).
  • 2.2 Threat vectors (message-based, removable device, vulnerable software, unsecure networks, default credentials, supply chain, human vectors…).
  • 2.5 Mitigation techniques (patching, hardening, least privilege, monitoring…).

How it classifies (deterministic and explainable)

  • Actor: each indicator adds weight to the actor profiles that use it. Highest total wins, but only if it beats the runner-up by min_margin. Otherwise the result is Undetermined: never guess.
  • Motivation: the first matching rule in an ordered list (more specific rules such as blackmail come before generic ones such as financial gain).
  • Vector: the observed initial-access indicator mapped to a 2.2 vector.
  • Mitigation: the vector's primary control, plus an actor-specific add-on.

Run it

python main.py lab 13

insight.objective: SY0-701 2.1 threat actors & motivations, 2.2 threat vectors, 2.5 mitigation techniques.
concepts: Attributes separate actors: internal vs external, resources/funding, level of sophistication.
Nation-states: well funded, patient (APT), espionage or war. Organized crime: money (ransomware, data sales, extortion).
Hacktivists want attention for a cause; insiders already have access; shadow IT is risk without malice.
Mitigate the VECTOR first (how they got in), then add controls suited to the ACTOR (how they will behave).
failure_modes: Attributing every incident to a nation-state: it inflates the response and hides basic hygiene gaps.
Ignoring shadow IT because 'nobody was malicious' when the data exposure is just as real.
Treating insiders like outsiders: perimeter controls do nothing against valid credentials.
Fixing the symptom (malware) but not the vector (USB policy, help-desk reset process).
ai_governance: An AI threat-intel agent should output 'Undetermined' rather than guess attribution; attribution errors drive bad decisions.
Require agents to list the indicators behind every classification so analysts can challenge them.
Agents summarising threat reports must treat that content as untrusted input (prompt injection lives in reports too).
Public attribution or law-enforcement referral is always a human decision.
exam_tips: 'Advanced persistent threat with large budget' = nation-state.
'Defaced site with a political message' = hacktivist. 'Unapproved cloud app' = shadow IT.
'Script kiddie' running public tools = unskilled attacker.
Vishing = voice, smishing = SMS, watering hole = compromise a site the victims trust.

labs.title: Lab 14 — Resilience & Recovery Planner
labs.objectives: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery (sites, replication, backups, RAID, power, testing)
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 3.4 Resilience and recovery in security architecture: high availability (load balancing vs clustering), site considerations (hot, warm, cold, geographic dispersion), platform diversity, multi-cloud, continuity of operations, capacity planning, testing (tabletop, fail over, simulation, parallel processing), backups (onsite/offsite, frequency, encryption, snapshots, recovery, replication, journaling), power (generators, UPS). RAID is part of the fault-tolerance toolbox.

Model

For each system we compute what the CURRENT design achieves in two events:

  • Host/storage failure: RTO = cluster failover time, or rebuild + restore. RPO = replication lag, or the backup interval. Restore time = data TB × hours/TB × multiplier (full 1.0, differential 1.5, incremental 2.5: incremental needs the full + every incremental since).
  • Site loss (only if required): needs an OFFSITE copy (replication or an offsite backup) AND a recovery site. RTO = site readiness (+ restore if the data isn't already replicated there).

Then disk fault tolerance (RAID), power (UPS + generator runtime) and testing (restore + DR test within 365 days) are checked. Every gap gets the cheapest catalog option that closes it.

Run it

python main.py lab 14

insight.objective: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery: sites, replication, backups, high availability, power, testing.
concepts: RPO is answered by backup frequency or replication; RTO by failover (clustering) or how fast a site can take over.
Hot = running and synced (expensive); warm = hardware ready, restore data; cold = space and power only.
Incremental backups are fastest to take but slowest to restore; differential is in between; full restores fastest.
RAID is availability, not backup: RAID1/5/10 survive one disk, RAID6 survives two, RAID0 survives none.
failure_modes: Nightly backups for a system the business assumed loses at most 4 hours of data.
Backups stored in the same building that floods.
A UPS with no generator, so it buys 10 minutes for a 4-hour outage.
A DR plan never tested; the first failover is during the real disaster.
ai_governance: An AI operations agent can trigger failover automatically only for pre-approved, tested runbooks.
Agents must not delete or shorten backup retention; backups are a protected control (Lab 5).
Use agents to run and record restore tests continuously, turning 'untested' into measured RTO/RPO.
Declaring a disaster (moving to the alternate site) stays a human decision.
exam_tips: Load balancing spreads load across active nodes; clustering adds failover. Both are high availability.
Geographic dispersion protects against regional disasters; multi-cloud protects against provider failure.
Testing types: tabletop (discussion), simulation, fail over, parallel processing (run both systems).
UPS = short-term power + clean shutdown; generator = long-term power.

labs.title: Lab 15 — Third-Party / Vendor Risk Assessor
labs.objectives: SY0-701 5.3 Third-party risk: assessment, selection, agreements, monitoring
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 5.3 Third-party risk assessment and management: vendor assessment (penetration testing, right-to-audit clause, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments, supply chain analysis), vendor selection (due diligence, conflict of interest), agreement types (SLA, MOA, MOU, MSA, WO/SOW, NDA, BPA), vendor monitoring, questionnaires, rules of engagement.

Model

inherent  = data sensitivity (1–4) × access level (1–4) × business criticality (1–3)
controls  = questionnaire score 0–100 % (yes = full weight, partial = half, unanswered = no)
residual  = inherent × (1 − 0.7 × controls)   (controls never remove ALL third-party risk)

Required contract clauses depend on what the vendor touches (data class, network/privileged access, partnership). Hard rules REJECT when:

  • the vendor handles confidential/regulated data and we can neither audit it (no right-to-audit clause) nor rely on an independent assessment;
  • a conflict of interest was not disclosed;
  • residual risk is HIGH.

Otherwise missing clauses or SLA shortfalls mean APPROVE_WITH_CONDITIONS, and a clean result means APPROVE. Each vendor also gets a monitoring cadence.

Run it

python main.py lab 15

insight.objective: SY0-701 5.3 Third-party risk: assessment, due diligence, agreement types, monitoring.
concepts: Inherent vendor risk comes from what the vendor touches: data sensitivity, network/privileged access, criticality.
Questionnaires, independent assessments (SOC 2, ISO 27001), pen tests and right-to-audit are how you VERIFY a vendor.
Agreements: MSA (umbrella terms), SOW/WO (specific work), SLA (measurable service), NDA, BPA (partnership), MOU/MOA (intent/agreement).
Vendor risk is continuous: monitor on a cadence matching the risk, and analyse their suppliers too (fourth parties).
failure_modes: Giving an HVAC contractor network access with no security requirements (how the 2013 Target breach began).
Signing a non-binding MOU where a binding agreement (BPA/MSA) was needed.
No right-to-audit and no independent assessment: you are trusting a marketing slide.
Skipping conflict-of-interest checks during selection.
ai_governance: AI vendors are third parties too: assess model providers for data use, retention, subprocessors and audit rights.
An AI procurement assistant can pre-score questionnaires, but approval and contract sign-off are human decisions.
Vendor answers are untrusted input: an agent reading questionnaires must not follow instructions embedded in them.
Keep agent-derived scores reproducible: same answers + same policy = same score, with every gap listed.
exam_tips: 'Allows the customer to inspect the vendor's security controls' = right-to-audit clause.
'Defines expected uptime and response times' = SLA. 'Umbrella contract for future work' = MSA.
MOU = intent, typically not legally binding. BPA = partner responsibilities and profit sharing.
Supply chain analysis looks at the vendor's own vendors and components (e.g. SBOM).

labs.title: Lab 16 — Security Control Classifier (category × type)
labs.objectives: SY0-701 1.1 Security control categories and types
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls: categories (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and control types (preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive).

How it classifies

Each description is scored against keyword/phrase weights in config/default_policies.json → control_classification (whole-word, case insensitive). Category and type are scored independently. The highest score wins only if it is UNIQUE; a tie or zero evidence returns Unclassified (deny by default: no guessing). Every result lists the phrases that drove it, so you can argue with the classifier, and improve the weights when it is wrong.

Run it

python main.py lab 16

insight.objective: SY0-701 1.1 Control categories (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and types.
concepts: CATEGORY = who/what implements it: technology (technical), people management and policy (managerial), people doing it (operational), the physical world (physical).
TYPE = what it does: prevent, deter, detect, correct, compensate for another control, or direct behaviour.
Every control has BOTH: a door lock is physical + preventive; a log review by managers is managerial + detective.
Compensating controls stand in when the primary control cannot be used (unpatchable server → isolate it).
failure_modes: Only buying preventive controls; nothing detects or corrects when prevention fails.
Writing policies (directive) with no technical enforcement or monitoring behind them.
Calling a compensating control 'temporary' and never removing the underlying gap.
Mapping controls inconsistently, so audits find gaps that were only labelling errors.
ai_governance: An AI GRC assistant can draft control mappings, but must show the evidence (phrases) behind each label.
Ambiguous controls should come back 'Unclassified' for a human, not be forced into a category.
AI agents themselves need controls of every type: preventive (allow-lists), detective (ledger), corrective (kill switch).
Policy statements for agents are directive; enforce them technically (Lab 5) or they are only wishes.
exam_tips: Signs: 'Authorized personnel only' = directive; 'trespassers will be prosecuted' = deterrent.
Backups/restore = corrective; logs/alarms/motion detectors = detective; firewall/locks = preventive.
Guards on patrol = operational (people performing the control).
Separation of duties is managerial; used in place of a missing control it becomes compensating.

labs.title: Lab 17 — PKI & Certificate Validator
labs.objectives: SY0-701 1.4 PKI: CAs, chains, CRL/OCSP, wildcard/SAN, self-signed, key length, pinning
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 1.4 Use appropriate cryptographic solutions: public key infrastructure (public/private keys, key escrow), certificates (certificate authorities, CRLs, OCSP, self-signed, third-party, root of trust, CSR generation, wildcard), key length, algorithms.

What it does

A browser-style validator for TLS certificate chains. Certificates are structured JSON records (subject, issuer, serial, validity, key, signature algorithm, CA flag, SAN, EKU, SPKI hash), so the trust rules are visible instead of buried in ASN.1. For each connection it checks, deny by default:

1. Path & trust: each cert's issuer is the next cert's subject; every issuer is a CA; the chain ends at (or is issued by) a trusted root. → INCOMPLETE_CHAIN, NOT_A_CA, SELF_SIGNED, UNTRUSTED_ROOT 2. Validity: every cert is inside its notBefore/notAfter window. → EXPIRED, NOT_YET_VALID; warnings EXPIRING_SOON, VALIDITY_TOO_LONG (> 398 days) 3. Hostname: matches a SAN entry (CN only if there is no SAN). A wildcard covers exactly ONE label: *.example.com matches a.example.com but not a.b.example.com or example.com. → HOSTNAME_MISMATCH 4. Strength: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits; SHA-2 signatures only. → WEAK_KEY, WEAK_SIGNATURE 5. Usage: the leaf's EKU must include serverAuth. → WRONG_KEY_USAGE 6. Revocation: OCSP status or the issuer's CRL. → REVOKED; no status available → REVOCATION_UNKNOWN (a warning under soft-fail, an error under hard-fail) 7. Pinning: if the app pins SPKI hashes, the presented key must match. → PIN_MISMATCH (classic sign of TLS interception)

Verdict: UNTRUSTED (any error) / TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS / TRUSTED.

Run it

python main.py lab 17

insight.objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and revocation.
concepts: Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) → intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2 signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
failure_modes: Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings, which makes MITM attacks invisible.
Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a revoked certificate look fine.
Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a calendar reminder, not automation.
ai_governance: Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be configured with 'verify=False'.
An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop the agent, not be retried around.
Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
exam_tips: 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of revoked serials' = CRL.
'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists several different names' = SAN.
'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything else chains to.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.2 Zero Trust (control plane vs data plane) and 4.6
| conditional access.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Control plane = Policy Engine (decides) + Policy Administrator
| (issues/revokes). Data plane = PEP + resources.
|   • Adaptive identity: the same user gets ALLOW, STEP_UP or DENY depending
| on real-time context.
|   • Threat scope reduction: tokens are short-lived and scoped to ONE
| resource + action.
|   • Never trust, always verify: the PEP re-validates on every request,
| even inside the network.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Treating 'on the VPN' or 'inside the LAN' as trusted (implicit trust
| zone).
|   • Long-lived or broadly-scoped tokens enable replay and lateral
| movement.
|   • MFA push approval alone treated as proof — MFA fatigue attacks bypass
| it.
|   • No revocation path: compromised sessions stay valid until expiry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Treat every AI agent as a non-human SUBJECT with its own identity,
| entitlements and device/workload posture.
|   • Agents should receive short-lived, narrowly-scoped tokens per task —
| never standing credentials.
|   • The PE should weigh agent-specific risk signals (anomalous call
| volume, new tool usage).
|   • The PA must be able to revoke an agent's tokens instantly (kill
| switch).
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Component that makes the access decision' => Policy Engine.
| 'Component that enforces it' => PEP.
|   • 'Establishes and terminates the session / issues tokens' => Policy
| Administrator.
|   • Zero Trust replaces perimeter trust with continuous, per-request
| verification.
|   • Microsegmentation and implicit trust zones are data-plane concepts.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| identity that approves it.

|   • Automation benefits: enforcing baselines, standard configurations,
| scaling securely, reaction time.
|   • Automation risks listed in 4.7: complexity, cost, single point of
| failure, technical debt, ongoing supportability.
|   • 'Guard rails' in 4.7 = automated limits that keep scripts/agents
| inside safe boundaries.
|   • Human-in-the-loop is the governance answer whenever impact is high and
| confidence is low.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative
| analysis, strategies, BIA).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE
| reduction > its annual cost.
|   • Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity),
| accept, or exception/exemption.
|   • RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how
| long you can be down (drives restore design).
|   • MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability =
| MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security
| theatre).
|   • Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead
| of transferring them.
|   • Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours,
| discovered only after an outage.
|   • Risks accepted informally with no owner, no expiry date and no
| register entry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a
| named human risk OWNER must accept.
|   • Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can
| be audited and challenged.
|   • AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure,
| prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
|   • Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a
| compromise. Price that in.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Expect arithmetic: AV $100k, EF 25%, ARO 2 → SLE $25k, ALE $50k.
|   • 'Purchasing cyber insurance' = transfer. 'Discontinuing the service' =
| avoid.
|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative
| analysis, strategies, BIA).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE
| reduction > its annual cost.
|   • Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity),
| accept, or exception/exemption.
|   • RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how
| long you can be down (drives restore design).
|   • MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability =
| MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security
| theatre).
|   • Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead
| of transferring them.
|   • Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours,
| discovered only after an outage.
|   • Risks accepted informally with no owner, no expiry date and no
| register entry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a
| named human risk OWNER must accept.
|   • Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can
| be audited and challenged.
|   • AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure,
| prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
|   • Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a
| compromise. Price that in.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Expect arithmetic: AV $100k, EF 25%, ARO 2 → SLE $25k, ALE $50k.
|   • 'Purchasing cyber insurance' = transfer. 'Discontinuing the service' =
| avoid.
|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative
| analysis, strategies, BIA).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE
| reduction > its annual cost.
|   • Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity),
| accept, or exception/exemption.
|   • RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how
| long you can be down (drives restore design).
|   • MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability =
| MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security
| theatre).
|   • Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead
| of transferring them.
|   • Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours,
| discovered only after an outage.
|   • Risks accepted informally with no owner, no expiry date and no
| register entry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a
| named human risk OWNER must accept.
|   • Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can
| be audited and challenged.
|   • AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure,
| prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
|   • Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a
| compromise. Price that in.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Expect arithmetic: AV $100k, EF 25%, ARO 2 → SLE $25k, ALE $50k.
|   • 'Purchasing cyber insurance' = transfer. 'Discontinuing the service' =
| avoid.
|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative
| analysis, strategies, BIA).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE
| reduction > its annual cost.
|   • Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity),
| accept, or exception/exemption.
|   • RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how
| long you can be down (drives restore design).
|   • MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability =
| MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security
| theatre).
|   • Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead
| of transferring them.
|   • Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours,
| discovered only after an outage.
|   • Risks accepted informally with no owner, no expiry date and no
| register entry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a
| named human risk OWNER must accept.
|   • Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can
| be audited and challenged.
|   • AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure,
| prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
|   • Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a
| compromise. Price that in.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Expect arithmetic: AV $100k, EF 25%, ARO 2 → SLE $25k, ALE $50k.
|   • 'Purchasing cyber insurance' = transfer. 'Discontinuing the service' =
| avoid.
|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative
| analysis, strategies, BIA).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE
| reduction > its annual cost.
|   • Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity),
| accept, or exception/exemption.
|   • RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how
| long you can be down (drives restore design).
|   • MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability =
| MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).

| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security
| theatre).
|   • Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead
| of transferring them.
|   • Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours,
| discovered only after an outage.

| register entry.

|   • An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a
| named human risk OWNER must accept.
|   • Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can
| be audited and challenged.
|   • AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure,
| prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
|   • Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a
| compromise. Price that in.

| avoid.
|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Incident IR-2026-0042 -------------------------------------------------
| EDR flags malware (invoice_Q4.pdf.exe) on WS-0142 beaconing to
| 45.155.205.233. The same IP brute-forced and logged in as jdoe, who then
| cleared the DC01 Security log.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Playbook: rookie  →  score 0/100  (grade F) -----------------------------

Timeline
#  Phase        Action
-  -----------  ------
1  detection    Triage the EDR alert and correlate it with SIEM data
2  containment  Pull the power plug on WS-0142
3  analysis     Copy suspicious files to a personal USB stick to look at later
4  eradication  Reimage WS-0142 from the golden image
5  recovery     Return WS-0142 to service; restore user data from known-good backup
6  analysis     Capture a RAM image of WS-0142 and hash it (SHA-256)
7  containment  Disable jdoe and revoke all sessions/tokens

Issues
Step  Code                Penalty  Detail
----  ------------------  -------  ------
2     ANTI_PATTERN        -10      'power_off': Destroys volatile evidence (RAM, network state, temp files)
2     EVIDENCE_DESTROYED  -20      'power_off' destroys uncollected evidence: ['CPU registers / cache', 'RAM, process table, network state', 'swap / temp files']
3     ANTI_PATTERN        -10      'copy_usb_unhashed': No hash, no write blocker, personal media: chain of custody is broken
3     CHAIN_OF_CUSTODY    -15      disk from WS-0142 acquired without a hash
4     MISSING_PREREQ      -15      'reimage' requires 'image_disk' first
4     MISSING_PREREQ      -15      'reimage' requires 'legal_hold' first
6     EVIDENCE_DESTROYED  -20      'capture_memory' tries to collect RAM, already destroyed by an earlier step
7     PHASE_ORDER         -10      containment ('disable_account') AFTER recovery: attacker had access the whole time
7     NO_LESSONS_LEARNED  -10      no lessons-learned review: the same incident will recur

Chain of custody
Evidence  Source  Host     Step  SHA-256  Status
--------  ------  -------  ----  -------  ------
EV-001    disk    WS-0142  3     —        FAIL
EV-002    RAM     WS-0142  6     —        FAIL

--- Playbook: expert  →  score 100/100  (grade A) ---------------------------

Timeline
#   Phase            Action
--  ---------------  ------
1   preparation      Maintain IR plan, contact list, jump kit and tested playbooks
2   detection        Triage the EDR alert and correlate it with SIEM data
3   detection        Declare an incident, assign an incident commander, open a case
4   analysis         Live response: record running processes, ARP cache and network connections
5   analysis         Capture a RAM image of WS-0142 and hash it (SHA-256)
6   analysis         Collect the pagefile, swap and temp files
7   containment      Network-isolate WS-0142 via EDR (power stays ON)
8   analysis         Place a legal hold; notify legal/privacy counsel
9   analysis         Scope the incident: find every affected host and account
10  analysis         Forensic disk image through a write blocker and hash it
11  analysis         Export firewall/SIEM/DC logs for the incident window and hash them
12  containment      Disable jdoe and revoke all sessions/tokens
13  containment      Block the IOC IP/domain at the firewall and DNS
14  eradication      Remove malware and persistence; patch the exploited weakness
15  eradication      Reset credentials for every exposed account (incl. service accounts)
16  eradication      Reimage WS-0142 from the golden image
17  recovery         Return WS-0142 to service; restore user data from known-good backup
18  recovery         Heightened monitoring for re-infection for 30 days
19  lessons_learned  Lessons-learned review: update playbooks and controls, write the final report
  • No issues found.

Chain of custody
Evidence  Source                         Host     Step  SHA-256            Status
--------  -----------------------------  -------  ----  -----------------  ------
EV-001    process table / network state  WS-0142  4     c06689da63253159…  VALID
EV-002    RAM                            WS-0142  5     f2448e065653efaf…  VALID
EV-003    swap / temp files              WS-0142  6     807de8bcdfade560…  VALID
EV-004    disk                           WS-0142  10    eb8a8fef6bc176ed…  VALID
EV-005    remote logs                    SIEM     11    fe3ed49bd6c1599e…  VALID

--- Custody ledger integrity ------------------------------------------------
  Expert custody ledger                          VALID  10 entries
  Ledger after someone rewrites who collected EV-001 TAMPERED  breaks at entry #1

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.8 Incident response process & digital forensics.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Lifecycle: preparation → detection → analysis → containment →
| eradication → recovery → lessons learned.
|   • Order of volatility (RFC 3227): registers/cache → RAM & network state
| → swap/temp → disk → remote logs → archives.
|   • Chain of custody: who collected what, when, with which hash, and every
| hand-off since. One gap and the evidence can be thrown out.
|   • A legal hold freezes deletion of relevant data the moment litigation
| is reasonably anticipated.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Pulling the plug 'to stop the malware': RAM-resident malware and
| network state are gone forever.
|   • Reimaging before imaging the disk: no root cause analysis, no evidence
| for law enforcement or insurers.
|   • Restoring service before eradication: re-infection from the
| persistence you never found.
|   • Skipping lessons learned, so the playbook never improves.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • AI responders should follow the SAME lifecycle; enforce phase gates
| (no eradication until containment is confirmed).
|   • Agents may collect evidence but must hash it at acquisition and write
| to an append-only custody ledger.
|   • Destructive actions (power off, reimage, delete) need human sign-off
| and must check that evidence was acquired first.
|   • Log every agent action into the incident timeline; the agent's own
| actions are evidence too.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'What should be collected first?' → the most volatile source available
| (usually RAM).
|   • 'Stop the spread' = containment; 'remove the malware' = eradication;
| 'return to normal' = recovery.
|   • 'Documents everyone who handled the evidence' = chain of custody.
|   • Tabletop exercise = discussion-based; simulation = hands-on practice
| of the plan.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

IMPOSSIBLE_TRAVEL (HIGH)        disable_account → asmith        REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL  REJECT by sec_architect   False positive: asmith confirmed travel; 95.165.12.80 is the new travel-VPN egress. Tune the impossible-travel rule.
SQL_INJECTION (HIGH)            block_ip → 185.220.101.45       ALLOW                   -                         RFC-AUTO-0001 → CAB APPROVE_WITH_CONDITIONS (rehearsal PASS)

--- Downstream controls -----------------------------------------------------
  IAM: accounts suspended                        OK  ['jdoe'] · 2 live session token(s) revoked
  Change control: emergency firewall RFC         APPROVE_WITH_CONDITIONS  CAB reviewed the agent's block-list change with a generated backout
  Incident response: hosts isolated              OK  ['ws-0142'] · 2 evidence items hashed into custody first

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.7 Automation & orchestration (SOAR) tying together
| 1.2, 1.3, 4.6, 4.8 and 4.9.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Detection, decision and execution are separate trust boundaries; no
| single component (or agent) owns all three.
|   • Every automated action is routed to the control that owns it: IAM for
| accounts, CAB for network changes, IR for hosts.
|   • Emergency changes still get an RFC, ECAB approval, a rehearsed backout
| and a post-implementation review.
|   • Human-in-the-loop on user-impacting actions turns false positives into
| rule-tuning instead of outages.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A SOAR playbook that disables accounts automatically locks out the CEO
| on a false positive.
|   • Automation that blocks IPs directly on the firewall, bypassing change
| control: no backout, no record.
|   • Isolating or wiping a host before capturing memory destroys the
| evidence that explains the breach.
|   • An over-privileged agent 'containing' an incident by changing the
| default firewall rule.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Give the SOC agent a narrow allow-list and let it PROPOSE; the
| Governor and humans DISPOSE.
|   • Make every downstream system (IAM, CAB, IR) enforce its own rules even
| for approved agent actions: defense in depth.
|   • Feed human rejections back as tuning data, e.g. the travel-VPN egress
| that triggered impossible travel.
|   • Measure the agent: precision of its proposals, how often humans
| overturn it, and blocked attempts.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • SOAR = Security Orchestration, Automation and Response: playbooks that
| act on SIEM alerts.
|   • Benefits in 4.7: efficiency, enforcing baselines, reaction time,
| workforce multiplier.
|   • Considerations in 4.7: complexity, cost, single point of failure,
| technical debt, ongoing supportability.
|   • Containment choices (isolate, segment, disable) must balance evidence
| preservation against spread.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  • V-09 [P1] No patch exists: apply compensating controls now (isolate, virtual patch/WAF, disable the feature) and track the vendor advisory

| Objective: SY0-701 4.3 Vulnerability management (analysis, prioritisation,
| remediation, validation) and 2.3 vulnerability types.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • CVSS is a severity score, not a risk score. Risk adds asset
| criticality, exposure and active exploitation (KEV).
|   • Remediation options: patch, segment/isolate, compensating controls,
| insurance, or a time-boxed exception.
|   • Validation closes the loop: rescan, audit or verify. A ticket marked
| 'done' is not proof.
|   • Assets missing from the inventory are the most dangerous: nobody
| patches what nobody owns.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Sorting by CVSS alone, so a 9.8 on a lab box outranks a KEV 7.5 on an
| internet-facing gateway.
|   • Exceptions with no expiry, approved by whoever asked, renewed forever.
|   • Waiting for a patch on a zero-day instead of applying compensating
| controls today.
|   • Closing findings without rescanning: the patch failed silently.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI triage agent may score and rank findings, but exceptions need an
| authorised human risk owner.
|   • Agents must take criticality and exposure from the CMDB, never infer
| or invent them; unknown assets mean worst case.
|   • Auto-patching agents go through change control (Lab 4) and must
| trigger a validation rescan afterwards.
|   • Log the agent's scoring inputs so a human can reproduce any priority
| it assigns.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • CVSS bands: 9.0–10 Critical, 7.0–8.9 High, 4.0–6.9 Medium, 0.1–3.9
| Low.
|   • 'Cannot patch, so add a control that reduces the risk' = compensating
| control.
|   • 'Formally accept a vulnerability for a defined time' =
| exception/exemption.
|   • TOC/TOU = race condition; malicious update = supply chain; no vendor
| fix yet = zero-day.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 4.3 Vulnerability management (analysis, prioritisation,
| remediation, validation) and 2.3 vulnerability types.

|   • CVSS is a severity score, not a risk score. Risk adds asset
| criticality, exposure and active exploitation (KEV).
|   • Remediation options: patch, segment/isolate, compensating controls,
| insurance, or a time-boxed exception.

| controls today.
|   • Closing findings without rescanning: the patch failed silently.

|   • An AI triage agent may score and rank findings, but exceptions need an
| authorised human risk owner.
|   • Agents must take criticality and exposure from the CMDB, never infer
| or invent them; unknown assets mean worst case.
|   • Auto-patching agents go through change control (Lab 4) and must
| trigger a validation rescan afterwards.
|   • Log the agent's scoring inputs so a human can reproduce any priority
| it assigns.

| Low.

| control.
|   • 'Formally accept a vulnerability for a defined time' =
| exception/exemption.
|   • TOC/TOU = race condition; malicious update = supply chain; no vendor
| fix yet = zero-day.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 4.3 Vulnerability management (analysis, prioritisation,

| Key Concepts
|   • CVSS is a severity score, not a risk score. Risk adds asset
| criticality, exposure and active exploitation (KEV).

| authorised human risk owner.

|   • Auto-patching agents go through change control (Lab 4) and must
| trigger a validation rescan afterwards.
|   • Log the agent's scoring inputs so a human can reproduce any priority
| it assigns.

| Low.
|   • 'Cannot patch, so add a control that reduces the risk' = compensating
| control.
|   • 'Formally accept a vulnerability for a defined time' =
| exception/exemption.
|   • TOC/TOU = race condition; malicious update = supply chain; no vendor
| fix yet = zero-day.

| Objective: SY0-701 4.5 Email security (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, gateways) and 2.2
| message-based threat vectors.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SPF authorises sending IPs for the ENVELOPE domain; DKIM signs the
| message for the d= domain.
|   • DMARC ties them to the visible From: SPF or DKIM must pass AND align
| with the From domain; p= says what to do on failure.
|   • Authentication proves where mail came from, not that it is safe: a
| lookalike domain can pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
|   • Content signals (impersonation, urgency, mismatched links, double
| extensions) catch what authentication cannot.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Publishing DMARC p=none forever: you can see the spoofing but never
| block it.
|   • Trusting an Authentication-Results header added by an untrusted hop.
|   • Allowing external mail whose display name matches the CEO, with no
| 'external sender' banner.
|   • Blocking .exe but not .pdf.exe, .iso, .lnk or macro-enabled documents.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail-triage agent may quarantine and add banners; releasing
| quarantined mail or allow-listing senders needs a human.
|   • Mail content is untrusted input: an email that tells the agent to
| 'mark this sender safe' is prompt injection.
|   • Agents must base verdicts on recomputed SPF/DKIM/DMARC, never on
| headers the sender controls.
|   • Log every agent verdict with its indicators so false positives can be
| tuned, as in the Lab 8 feedback loop.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • SPF = which servers may send · DKIM = digital signature on the message
| · DMARC = policy + alignment + reporting.
|   • BEC/impersonation: 'CEO' from a free-mail address asking for a wire
| transfer or changed bank details.
|   • Typosquatting / brand impersonation: micros0ft-support.com,
| paypa1.com.
|   • Secure email gateways enforce these checks at the perimeter; S/MIME
| provides end-to-end signing/encryption.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 3.2 secure infrastructure (zones, screened subnets) and
| 4.5 firewall rules / ACLs.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Rules are evaluated top-down, first match wins, so ORDER is part of
| the security policy.
|   • Implicit deny: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked. Make it
| explicit and logged.
|   • Screened subnet (DMZ): internet → DMZ on published ports only; DMZ →
| internal only to specific back-end services.
|   • Least privilege for networks: specific source, destination, protocol
| and port, never 'any' for convenience.
|
