|   • A 'temporary' any/any rule added during troubleshooting and never
| removed.
|   • A new deny rule appended to the bottom, below an allow that already
| matches the traffic (shadowed).
|   • RDP or SMB opened to the internet 'for a vendor'.
|   • Rule sets nobody can explain because rules carry no owner, ticket or
| comment.

|   • An AI firewall agent should submit proposed rules to this audit +
| change control (Lab 4) before deployment.
|   • Block agents from creating any/any or segmentation-violating rules
| (Lab 5 OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_RULE).
|   • Agents must never edit the default-deny or other immutable rules (Lab
| 5 rule 0).
|   • Require every agent-created rule to carry a ticket reference and an
| expiry for temporary access.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Rule never matches because an earlier rule catches the traffic' =
| shadowed rule.
|   • 'Last rule of an ACL that blocks everything else' = implicit deny.
|   • Screened subnet = DMZ; place public-facing servers there, not on the
| internal network.
|   • Fail-closed (secure) vs fail-open (available): know which a
| firewall/IPS should use for the scenario.

|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.

| detect with periodic scans.

| both appear in 4.1.

| Objective: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain;
| hardening targets and techniques.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration; deploy it
| with GPO/MDM/config management, then measure drift.
|   • Hardening = reduce attack surface: remove unneeded services, enforce
| password/lockout policy, enable host firewall, EDR and auditing.
|   • Unknown is non-compliant: a setting the scanner can't read is treated
| as failed until proven otherwise.
|   • Exceptions are documented, ticketed, compensated and time-boxed, never
| silent.

|   • Someone re-enables Print Spooler on a domain controller 'to print one

| control with rollback (Lab 4).
|   • Agents must never weaken a baseline (disable firewall/EDR/auditing);
| that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
|   • Drift alerts are a great agent job: detect, explain, open a ticket,
| attach the remediation step.
|   • Approving a deviation (exception) stays a human decision with an
| expiry date.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
|   • Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic
| hardening.
|   • Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline;
| detect with periodic scans.
|   • Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control)
| both appear in 4.1.

--- Classification ----------------------------------------------------------

Threat actor · motivation · vector
ID    Scenario                             Actor               Motivation                         Initial access vector
----  -----------------------------------  ------------------  ---------------------------------  ---------------------
T-01  Quiet theft at a defense contractor  Nation-state        Espionage                          Watering hole (compromised trusted website)
T-02  Hospital ransomware                  Organized crime     Financial gain                     Message-based: email phishing
T-03  City website defaced                 Hacktivist          Philosophical/political beliefs    Vulnerable software / open service port
T-04  Backups wiped by an administrator    Insider threat      Revenge                            Valid account / authorized access
T-05  Lobby cameras hijacked               Unskilled attacker  Disruption/chaos                   Default credentials
T-06  Customer list on a public share      Shadow IT           Convenience (no malicious intent)  Unsanctioned cloud service
T-07  USB sticks in the parking lot        Organized crime     Financial gain                     Removable device
T-08  Executive mailbox extortion          Organized crime     Blackmail                          Voice call (vishing / pretexting)

--- Why, and what to do -----------------------------------------------------
T-01 Quiet theft at a defense contractor
  • Actor evidence: high_funding (+3), advanced_tools (+3), long_dwell_time (+3), targets_government_or_defense (+3), espionage_data_theft (+2), score 14 vs next best Organized crime 1
  • Motivation: 'espionage_data_theft' → Espionage
  • Mitigate the vector: Patch browsers/plugins, DNS/web filtering, isolate browsing
  • For this actor also: Assume persistence: threat hunting, segmentation, and intel sharing (ISAC)
T-02 Hospital ransomware
  • Actor evidence: ransomware (+3), demands_payment (+3), financial_data_targeted (+2), score 8 vs next best Hacktivist 0
  • Motivation: 'demands_payment' → Financial gain
  • Mitigate the vector: Email gateway with DMARC enforcement + security awareness training
  • For this actor also: Offline/immutable backups and an extortion response plan
T-03 City website defaced
  • Actor evidence: political_message (+3), public_claim (+3), defacement_or_ddos (+3), score 9 vs next best Insider threat 0
  • Motivation: 'political_message' → Philosophical/political beliefs
  • Mitigate the vector: Patch management + reduce exposed attack surface
  • For this actor also: DDoS protection and monitoring of public-facing assets
T-04 Backups wiped by an administrator
  • Actor evidence: authorized_access_abused (+4), recently_disgruntled (+3), internal_origin (+3), after_hours_access (+1), score 11 vs next best Shadow IT 1
  • Motivation: 'recently_disgruntled' → Revenge
  • Mitigate the vector: Least privilege + separation of duties + UEBA monitoring
  • For this actor also: Offboarding/JML hygiene and data loss prevention
T-05 Lobby cameras hijacked
  • Actor evidence: public_exploit_tools (+3), noisy_attack (+3), low_sophistication (+3), bragging (+2), score 11 vs next best Hacktivist 0
  • Motivation: 'bragging' → Disruption/chaos
  • Mitigate the vector: Hardening: change default credentials, disable unused accounts
  • For this actor also: Basic hygiene closes most of the doors (patching, defaults, MFA)
T-06 Customer list on a public share
  • Actor evidence: unapproved_service (+4), no_malicious_intent (+4), internal_origin (+1), score 9 vs next best Insider threat 3
  • Motivation: 'no_malicious_intent' → Convenience (no malicious intent)
  • Mitigate the vector: CASB discovery/blocking + acceptable use policy
  • For this actor also: Give people a sanctioned alternative so they stop working around IT
T-07 USB sticks in the parking lot
  • Actor evidence: sells_data (+3), financial_data_targeted (+2), score 5 vs next best Hacktivist 0
  • Motivation: 'sells_data' → Financial gain
  • Mitigate the vector: Disable USB mass storage + application allow list
  • For this actor also: Offline/immutable backups and an extortion response plan
T-08 Executive mailbox extortion
  • Actor evidence: threatens_to_leak_unless_paid (+3), demands_payment (+3), score 6 vs next best Hacktivist 0
  • Motivation: 'threatens_to_leak_unless_paid' → Blackmail
  • Mitigate the vector: Help-desk caller verification procedure before any reset
  • For this actor also: Offline/immutable backups and an extortion response plan

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 2.1 threat actors & motivations, 2.2 threat vectors,
| 2.5 mitigation techniques.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Attributes separate actors: internal vs external, resources/funding,
| level of sophistication.
|   • Nation-states: well funded, patient (APT), espionage or war. Organized
| crime: money (ransomware, data sales, extortion).
|   • Hacktivists want attention for a cause; insiders already have access;
| shadow IT is risk without malice.
|   • Mitigate the VECTOR first (how they got in), then add controls suited
| to the ACTOR (how they will behave).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Attributing every incident to a nation-state: it inflates the response
| and hides basic hygiene gaps.
|   • Ignoring shadow IT because 'nobody was malicious' when the data
| exposure is just as real.
|   • Treating insiders like outsiders: perimeter controls do nothing
| against valid credentials.
|   • Fixing the symptom (malware) but not the vector (USB policy, help-desk
| reset process).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI threat-intel agent should output 'Undetermined' rather than
| guess attribution; attribution errors drive bad decisions.
|   • Require agents to list the indicators behind every classification so
| analysts can challenge them.
|   • Agents summarising threat reports must treat that content as untrusted
| input (prompt injection lives in reports too).
|   • Public attribution or law-enforcement referral is always a human
| decision.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Advanced persistent threat with large budget' = nation-state.
|   • 'Defaced site with a political message' = hacktivist. 'Unapproved
| cloud app' = shadow IT.
|   • 'Script kiddie' running public tools = unskilled attacker.
|   • Vishing = voice, smishing = SMS, watering hole = compromise a site the
| victims trust.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery: sites, replication, backups,
| high availability, power, testing.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • RPO is answered by backup frequency or replication; RTO by failover
| (clustering) or how fast a site can take over.
|   • Hot = running and synced (expensive); warm = hardware ready, restore
| data; cold = space and power only.
|   • Incremental backups are fastest to take but slowest to restore;
| differential is in between; full restores fastest.
|   • RAID is availability, not backup: RAID1/5/10 survive one disk, RAID6
| survives two, RAID0 survives none.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Nightly backups for a system the business assumed loses at most 4
| hours of data.
|   • Backups stored in the same building that floods.
|   • A UPS with no generator, so it buys 10 minutes for a 4-hour outage.
|   • A DR plan never tested; the first failover is during the real
| disaster.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI operations agent can trigger failover automatically only for
| pre-approved, tested runbooks.
|   • Agents must not delete or shorten backup retention; backups are a
| protected control (Lab 5).
|   • Use agents to run and record restore tests continuously, turning
| 'untested' into measured RTO/RPO.
|   • Declaring a disaster (moving to the alternate site) stays a human
| decision.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Load balancing spreads load across active nodes; clustering adds
| failover. Both are high availability.
|   • Geographic dispersion protects against regional disasters; multi-cloud
| protects against provider failure.
|   • Testing types: tabletop (discussion), simulation, fail over, parallel
| processing (run both systems).
|   • UPS = short-term power + clean shutdown; generator = long-term power.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Recovery capability

--- Step 2 — Gaps and cheapest fixes ----------------------------------------
api-gateway — GAPS
  • SITE: cold site recovery takes 168h > target 4h
  • TEST: DR failover last tested 2025-03-13 (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Use a hot site (ready in 1h, $500,000/yr)
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO
file-server — GAPS
  • RTO: host failure takes 4.75h (rebuild + full restore) > target 4h
  • RPO: up to 4h of data lost > target 15m
  • SITE: no offsite copy of the data (no replication, backups kept onsite)
  • DISK: RAID10 tolerates 1 disk failure(s) < required 2
  • TEST: DR failover last tested 2025-03-13 (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Add active-passive clustering (failover 15m, $30,000/yr)
  • → Add asynchronous replication (RPO 15m, $40,000/yr)
  • → Keep an offsite/cloud backup copy (3-2-1) or replicate to the recovery site
  • → Rebuild storage as RAID6 (tolerates 2, 67% usable capacity)
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO
edge-fw — GAPS
  • RPO: up to 12h of data lost > target 1h
  • SITE RPO: after a site loss up to 12h of data is lost > target 1h
  • TEST: backup restore last tested 2025-06-21 (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Back up at least every 1h (snapshots/journaling between full backups)
  • → Schedule a restore test and record the measured RTO/RPO
web-frontend — GAPS
  • RTO: host failure takes 11.5h (rebuild + incremental restore) > target 4h
  • SITE: cold site recovery takes 168h > target 4h
  • POWER: UPS + generator run 0h < required 4h
  • → Add active-passive clustering (failover 15m, $30,000/yr)
  • → Use a hot site (ready in 1h, $500,000/yr)
  • → Add a generator (a UPS only bridges minutes)

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery: sites, replication, backups,
| high availability, power, testing.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • RPO is answered by backup frequency or replication; RTO by failover
| (clustering) or how fast a site can take over.
|   • Hot = running and synced (expensive); warm = hardware ready, restore
| data; cold = space and power only.
|   • Incremental backups are fastest to take but slowest to restore;
| differential is in between; full restores fastest.
|   • RAID is availability, not backup: RAID1/5/10 survive one disk, RAID6
| survives two, RAID0 survives none.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Nightly backups for a system the business assumed loses at most 4
| hours of data.
|   • Backups stored in the same building that floods.
|   • A UPS with no generator, so it buys 10 minutes for a 4-hour outage.
|   • A DR plan never tested; the first failover is during the real
| disaster.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI operations agent can trigger failover automatically only for
| pre-approved, tested runbooks.
|   • Agents must not delete or shorten backup retention; backups are a
| protected control (Lab 5).
|   • Use agents to run and record restore tests continuously, turning
| 'untested' into measured RTO/RPO.
|   • Declaring a disaster (moving to the alternate site) stays a human
| decision.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Load balancing spreads load across active nodes; clustering adds
| failover. Both are high availability.
|   • Geographic dispersion protects against regional disasters; multi-cloud
| protects against provider failure.
|   • Testing types: tabletop (discussion), simulation, fail over, parallel
| processing (run both systems).
|   • UPS = short-term power + clean shutdown; generator = long-term power.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  • 3 questionnaire gap(s), e.g. Q05 Incident response plan tested in the last 12 months: partial
VN-5 NetOps MSP → REJECT · monitoring: quarterly reviews + continuous monitoring
  • REJECT: conflict of interest not disclosed/cleared: due diligence failed
  • CONDITION: residual risk 13.32 is MEDIUM: agree a remediation plan for the questionnaire gaps

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.3 Third-party risk: assessment, due diligence,
| agreement types, monitoring.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Inherent vendor risk comes from what the vendor touches: data
| sensitivity, network/privileged access, criticality.
|   • Questionnaires, independent assessments (SOC 2, ISO 27001), pen tests
| and right-to-audit are how you VERIFY a vendor.
|   • Agreements: MSA (umbrella terms), SOW/WO (specific work), SLA
| (measurable service), NDA, BPA (partnership), MOU/MOA (intent/agreement).
|   • Vendor risk is continuous: monitor on a cadence matching the risk, and
| analyse their suppliers too (fourth parties).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Giving an HVAC contractor network access with no security requirements
| (how the 2013 Target breach began).
|   • Signing a non-binding MOU where a binding agreement (BPA/MSA) was
| needed.
|   • No right-to-audit and no independent assessment: you are trusting a
| marketing slide.
|   • Skipping conflict-of-interest checks during selection.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • AI vendors are third parties too: assess model providers for data use,
| retention, subprocessors and audit rights.
|   • An AI procurement assistant can pre-score questionnaires, but approval
| and contract sign-off are human decisions.
|   • Vendor answers are untrusted input: an agent reading questionnaires
| must not follow instructions embedded in them.
|   • Keep agent-derived scores reproducible: same answers + same policy =
| same score, with every gap listed.
| 
| Exam Tips

| right-to-audit clause.
|   • 'Defines expected uptime and response times' = SLA. 'Umbrella contract
| for future work' = MSA.
|   • MOU = intent, typically not legally binding. BPA = partner
| responsibilities and profit sharing.
|   • Supply chain analysis looks at the vendor's own vendors and components
| (e.g. SBOM).
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.3 Third-party risk: assessment, due diligence,
| agreement types, monitoring.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Inherent vendor risk comes from what the vendor touches: data
| sensitivity, network/privileged access, criticality.
|   • Questionnaires, independent assessments (SOC 2, ISO 27001), pen tests
| and right-to-audit are how you VERIFY a vendor.
|   • Agreements: MSA (umbrella terms), SOW/WO (specific work), SLA
| (measurable service), NDA, BPA (partnership), MOU/MOA (intent/agreement).
|   • Vendor risk is continuous: monitor on a cadence matching the risk, and
| analyse their suppliers too (fourth parties).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Giving an HVAC contractor network access with no security requirements
| (how the 2013 Target breach began).
|   • Signing a non-binding MOU where a binding agreement (BPA/MSA) was
| needed.
|   • No right-to-audit and no independent assessment: you are trusting a
| marketing slide.
|   • Skipping conflict-of-interest checks during selection.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • AI vendors are third parties too: assess model providers for data use,
| retention, subprocessors and audit rights.
|   • An AI procurement assistant can pre-score questionnaires, but approval
| and contract sign-off are human decisions.
|   • Vendor answers are untrusted input: an agent reading questionnaires
| must not follow instructions embedded in them.
|   • Keep agent-derived scores reproducible: same answers + same policy =
| same score, with every gap listed.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Allows the customer to inspect the vendor's security controls' =
| right-to-audit clause.
|   • 'Defines expected uptime and response times' = SLA. 'Umbrella contract
| for future work' = MSA.
|   • MOU = intent, typically not legally binding. BPA = partner
| responsibilities and profit sharing.
|   • Supply chain analysis looks at the vendor's own vendors and components
| (e.g. SBOM).
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

|   • No right-to-audit and no independent assessment: you are trusting a
| marketing slide.
|   • Skipping conflict-of-interest checks during selection.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • AI vendors are third parties too: assess model providers for data use,
| retention, subprocessors and audit rights.
|   • An AI procurement assistant can pre-score questionnaires, but approval
| and contract sign-off are human decisions.
|   • Vendor answers are untrusted input: an agent reading questionnaires
| must not follow instructions embedded in them.
|   • Keep agent-derived scores reproducible: same answers + same policy =
| same score, with every gap listed.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Allows the customer to inspect the vendor's security controls' =
| right-to-audit clause.
|   • 'Defines expected uptime and response times' = SLA. 'Umbrella contract
| for future work' = MSA.
|   • MOU = intent, typically not legally binding. BPA = partner
| responsibilities and profit sharing.
|   • Supply chain analysis looks at the vendor's own vendors and components
| (e.g. SBOM).

--- Step 2 — Why, and how to fix it -----------------------------------------
P-01 Healthy e-commerce site → TRUSTED
  • Valid chain, name, strength, usage and revocation status.
P-02 API certificate nobody renewed → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR EXPIRED: 'api.delzarsolutions.com' expired on 2026-10-31
  • Fix: Renew and automate renewal (ACME); monitor expiry dates.
P-03 Wildcard stretched one level too far → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR HOSTNAME_MISMATCH: 'dev.portal.delzarsolutions.com' is not covered by ['*.delzarsolutions.com', 'delzarsolutions.com']
  • Fix: Re-issue with the correct SAN entries (a wildcard covers only one label).
P-04 Server forgot to send its intermediate → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR INCOMPLETE_CHAIN: issuer 'GlobalTrust TLS CA 3' was not sent and is not a trusted root (missing intermediate)
  • Fix: Configure the server to send the full chain (leaf + intermediates).
P-05 Self-signed admin console → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR SELF_SIGNED: 'admin.internal' is self-signed and not in the trust store
  • WARNING VALIDITY_TOO_LONG: leaf is valid for 3652 days (> 398)
  • WARNING REVOCATION_UNKNOWN: no OCSP answer and no CRL for the leaf; status cannot be confirmed
  • Fix: Issue the certificate from your internal CA (or a public CA); don't train users to click through warnings.
P-06 Certificate revoked after key compromise → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR REVOKED: 'vpn.delzarsolutions.com' (serial 1006) is revoked (CRL from Delzar Issuing CA 1)
  • Fix: Replace the certificate now; it was revoked (often key compromise). Investigate the key.
P-07 Legacy appliance with old crypto → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR WEAK_KEY: 'printer.delzarsolutions.com' uses RSA-1024 (< 2048)
  • ERROR WEAK_SIGNATURE: 'printer.delzarsolutions.com' is signed with sha1WithRSAEncryption
  • Fix: Generate a new key pair (RSA ≥ 2048 or EC P-256+) and a new CSR.
P-08 Mobile banking app behind a TLS-inspection proxy → UNTRUSTED
  • WARNING EXPIRING_SOON: leaf expires in 28 days (2026-12-01)
  • ERROR PIN_MISMATCH: presented key 0dd1e57ab1e5… is not one of the app's pinned keys
  • Fix: Treat as interception: verify the network path / proxy; never disable the pin to 'make it work'.
P-09 Renewal due, revocation server unreachable → TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS
  • WARNING EXPIRING_SOON: leaf expires in 17 days (2026-11-20)
  • WARNING REVOCATION_UNKNOWN: no OCSP answer and no CRL for the leaf; status cannot be confirmed
  • Fix: Enable OCSP stapling so clients always get a fresh revocation status.
P-10 A leaf certificate used to sign another → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR NOT_A_CA: 'shop.delzarsolutions.com' signed 'store.delzarsolutions.com' but is not a CA (basicConstraints CA:FALSE)
  • Fix: Re-issue from a real CA: a leaf certificate (CA:FALSE) cannot sign other certificates.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  • Valid chain, name, strength, usage and revocation status.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 2 — Why, and how to fix it -----------------------------------------
P-01 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR WRONG_KEY_USAGE: leaf EKU ['clientAuth'] does not allow TLS server authentication
  • Fix: Request a certificate with the serverAuth extended key usage.
P-02 Generated connection → TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS

  • Fix: Enable OCSP stapling so clients always get a fresh revocation status.

  • Fix: Re-issue with the correct SAN entries (a wildcard covers only one label).
P-04 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR SELF_SIGNED: 'api.acme-partner.com' is self-signed and not in the trust store
  • Fix: Issue the certificate from your internal CA (or a public CA); don't train users to click through warnings.
P-05 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED

  • Fix: Check the server clock / NTP and the certificate's notBefore date.
P-06 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR HOSTNAME_MISMATCH: 'a.b.example.org' is not covered by ['vpn.example.org']
  • ERROR REVOKED: 'vpn.example.org' (serial 3006) is revoked (CRL from Delzar Issuing CA 1)
  • Fix: Replace the certificate now; it was revoked (often key compromise). Investigate the key.
P-07 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR REVOKED: 'www.delzarsolutions.com' (serial 3007) is revoked (CRL from Delzar Issuing CA 1)
  • Fix: Replace the certificate now; it was revoked (often key compromise). Investigate the key.
P-08 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR HOSTNAME_MISMATCH: 'dev.portal.acme-partner.com' is not covered by ['api.acme-partner.com', '*.acme-partner.com']
  • Fix: Re-issue with the correct SAN entries (a wildcard covers only one label).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.

| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.

| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one

| revoked certificate look fine.

| calendar reminder, not automation.

| configured with 'verify=False'.
